en.title: Can the Saved Fall Away? The Doctrine of Final Perseverance
en.question: Calvinists teach that true believers will inevitably persevere to the end. Does the Catholic Church agree that the saved cannot ultimately fall away?

answer.summary:
> "Not he who begins, but he who perseveres to the end will be saved." — St. Jerome, Commentary on Matthew 10

The Catholic doctrine of final perseverance holds that a justified person can and must persevere to the end of life in a state of grace to attain salvation, and that this perseverance is itself a gift of God's grace — not a human achievement. The Church agrees with Calvinism that perseverance is entirely dependent on God's sustaining grace, but firmly denies the Calvinist claim that the elect are guaranteed to persevere unconditionally and cannot ultimately fall away. The difference is not about the necessity of grace but about whether God's grace irresistibly ensures perseverance or whether a genuinely free human person can ultimately reject it even after having received it.

Jesus's words are decisive: "He who endures to the end will be saved" (Matthew 10:22, 24:13). The conditional structure — endurance as a condition of salvation — is incompatible with guaranteed, unconditional security. In the parable of the Sower (Matthew 13:20–21), Jesus describes people who "receive the word with joy" but fall away "when tribulation or persecution arises." Luke 8:13 adds that "they believe for a while, and in time of temptation fall away." These are not people who never truly believed; they are people who genuinely received the word but did not persevere. Paul himself writes: "Having begun with the Spirit, are you now ending with the flesh?" (Galatians 3:3) — a question that only makes sense if such a fall is genuinely possible.

Hebrews 6:4–6 is the most explicit passage: those "who have been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit" — unambiguously describing regenerate Christians — can nevertheless "fall away." The author does not describe this as a theoretical impossibility prevented by divine irresistibility but as a real danger requiring warning. Hebrews 3:12–14 exhorts: "Take care, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God." An exhortation without genuine force is empty — God does not warn against impossibilities.

The key theological distinction is between **sufficient grace** (which God offers to all the justified, enough to persevere) and **efficacious grace** (which actually produces perseverance). The Church teaches that God offers every justified person sufficient grace to persevere, and that He predestines the elect from eternity. But the Church does not teach that this predestination renders impossible the defection of any particular individual known to be justified in this life. Only God knows with certainty who the final elect are. The Council of Trent (Session VI, Chapter 13) defined that no one can know with the certainty of faith that they are among the predestined, apart from special revelation — not because God's grace is weak, but because the human will remains genuinely free to its final breath.

Final perseverance is therefore a gift to be prayed for, hoped for, and cooperated with — not a guaranteed possession to be presumed upon. The Catechism (CCC 2016) states: "The grace of final perseverance... is a gift of God which we can receive only from him." The Church counsels what the Catechism calls "holy fear" — not anxiety, but a sober awareness that salvation is worked out in the ongoing drama of a free will sustained by grace until death.
